subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Prospect Theory in Marketing
description: A micro-lesson that makes Prospect Theory in Marketing usable.

hook.text: 'Get $5 off' works differently than 'avoid a $5 surcharge.' Marketers pick the frame that sells.

buildup.text: Loss-framed messages drive action when the stakes feel personal. Gain frames work for new opportunities.

discovery.text: Prospect theory is the hidden engine of pricing. Decoys, anchors, bundles, and discounts all exploit its curves.

twist.text: The $999 price tag anchors you below $1,000. The $19.99 feels closer to $19 than $20. Pennies move perception.

climax.text: Every price you see is framed. Knowing the frame doesn't make you immune, but it gives you a fighting chance.

quiz.question: Why is $999 used instead of $1,000?
options: It's easier to calculate tax on
It anchors perception below the $1,000 threshold

details.summary: Marketers exploit prospect theory by framing prices as discounts from higher reference points, bundling losses into single payments, and using free trials that create endowment effects when the trial ends and the product feels like a loss to give up.
details.whyItMatters: Nearly every pricing and promotion strategy in modern marketing is built on prospect theory insights. Understanding these tactics helps consumers recognize manipulation and helps marketers design more effective campaigns.
takeaways: Reference pricing creates artificial gains by showing original prices
Free trials exploit the endowment effect and loss aversion at cancellation
Bundling reduces the pain of paying by combining multiple costs

faq.question: Why do stores always show the original price next to sale prices?
faq.answer: The original price sets a reference point that makes the sale price feel like a gain. A shirt at $40 feels ordinary, but the same shirt marked down from $80 to $40 feels like winning $40. The reference point creates perceived value.

faq.question: How do free trials use prospect theory?
faq.answer: During the trial you develop ownership and habits around the product. When the trial ends, canceling feels like a loss rather than a return to normal. Loss aversion makes the pain of losing access stronger than the pain of paying.
